div.p: The extractive industry plays an important role in Greece's economy. Nevertheless, in years to come, Greek mining enterprises may face economic losses due to climate change. This study aimed, for the first time, to explore the perceptions and attitudes of Greek mining practitioners towards climate change, and to investigate existing and planned climate-change adaptation and mitigation actions. To this end, a bottom-up survey based on face-to-face interviews of key practitioners from all of the operational mines in the Cyclades region of Greece was conducted. According to the results, mining enterprises are already experiencing negative impacts of extreme weather events. The major vulnerabilities of these enterprises relate to the management of excess rainwater, strong winds, and unusually high or low temperatures. However, the adaptation actions implemented by the companies are not systematic or are not always labeled as such, while most of their mitigation actions are performed to improve energy efficiency and achieve better economic outcomes. Even though the mining sector perceives climate change to be a threat to its activities, it has not invested the resources required to adapt to the future climate. Further, scientific knowledge of this phenomenon is limited among mining practitioners. To this end, governments and institutional stakeholders should promote climate-change awareness and disseminate successful adaptative actions to increase the future resilience of the mining sector.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The first working group of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) declares in its Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) that the observed changes in the climate that are attributable to human activities are snow melting and reduced snow cover, permafrost thawing, increased air temperatures, rising sea levels, and more frequent temperature extremes, droughts, wildfires, intense precipitation episodes, flooding, hurricanes, tornadoes, and other extreme weather events (Stocker et al. 2013).

These phenomena affect the mining sector in many ways. Intense rainfall negatively affects mine geomorphology and drainage, causing issues such as stability problems with mine benches, waste disposal areas, and tailings dams; pond, dam, reservoir, ditch, and culvert overflows; damage to or losses of machinery and equipment; damage to haul roads; disruptions to operations; and an increased risk of personnel injury (Damigos 2012;Duerden et al. 2014;Field et al. 2014;Mason et al. 2013;Mason and Giurco 2013;Sharma et al. 2013;Sharma and Franks 2013;Stratos Inc. 2011). On the other hand, prolonged droughts may adversely affect mine water withdrawals and exacerbate the water-use pressure on water-intensive processes (ICMM 2013(ICMM , 2014;;Mason and Giurco 2013;Prior et al. 2007), causing an increased need for irrigation of rehabilitation works as well Communicated by Christos Giannakopoulos, Guest Editor.

An increased temperature along with decreased rainfall may impact water-dependent mines (Nelson and Schuchard 2011) as well as water-dependent mine tailings facilities (Bjelkevik 2005). Unusually high temperatures may negatively affect the mining industry by reducing productivity, hindering rational decision making, increasing personnel absenteeism, and heightening the risk of heat-related illnesses such as malaria (ICMM 2013;Nelson and Schuchard 2011;Prior et al. 2007). Moreover, temperature rises in the high latitudes could induce permafrost thawing, causing infrastructural problems and shrinking the ice road season, thus increasing arctic mine transportation costs (Etkin et al. 1998;Ford et al. 2010;Pearce et al. 2009Pearce et al. , 2011)). Extremely windy and rainy conditions could lead to overtopping of toxic wastes or uncontrolled discharges from tailing dams (Bjelkevik 2005;Sharma et al. 2013), as well as problems with electric power generation and transmission, which represent a significant risk to mining companies (Nelson and Schuchard 2011;Smith 2013). Finally, rising sea levels and storm surges may affect port facilities, leading to supply chain disruptions (Becker et al. 2011;Kontogianni et al. 2018;Nelson and Schuchard 2011;Prior et al. 2007;Sarwar 2014). These effects of climate change could have significant economic impacts on the mining industry. For instance, the Diavik Diamond Mine in Canada's Northwest Territories incurred extra transportation costs of CAD 11.25 million due to a shortened ice road season in 2006 (Pearce et al. 2009). In 2008, floods cost Ensham Coal Mine in Central Queensland (Australia) around AUD 300 million and several months of lost production (Sharma and Franks 2013). Further, the devastating floods of January 2011 in eastern Australia caused serious disruptions to 45 of the 57 coal mines in Queensland and resulted in a 32% drop in Australia's metallurgical coal exports in Q1 of 2011, equivalent to a loss of around AUD 2.5 billion in export earnings (ABARES 2011;Odell et al. 2018). Further, Damigos (2012) performed a top-down study assessing the impacts of climate change in the Greek mining sector and estimated that Greece's mining industry could face economic losses of as much as USD 0.8 billion due to climate change. Nevertheless, it is worth mentioning the fact that many companies tend to hide their knowledge of previous adverse effects of climate change because their management teams are afraid of discouraging investors, a possible market share drop, or even damage to the company's public image (ICMM 2013). Of course, there are certain situations where climate change may be advantageous to the mining sector; one example is arctic environments, where expected temperature rises and reduced snow coverage could increase the possibility of year-round prospecting, operations, and shipping (Nelson and Schuchard 2011;Prior et al. 2007;Prowse et al. 2009;Rosen 2016; The Committee for Greenlandic Mineral Resources to the Benefit of Society 2014).

As Ford et al. (2010) note, the scientific community has alarmed the mining sector with their predictions of climaterelated impacts since 2000. Yet, public pressure and strict carbon tax schemes have only pushed mining companies towards mitigation strategies. This mitigation-focused strategy prevailed in the First Position Statement on Climate Change of an institutional stakeholder, the International Council on Mining & Metals (ICMM), in 2006(ICMM 2006), but the position of that council changed a few years later, prompting mining companies to implement adaptation actions (ICMM 2009(ICMM , 2011)).

The argument of Ford et al. (2010) regarding climate change-that perceptions and behaviors or actions are interlinked-has led to various scientific efforts around the world to explore how the mining sector perceives, experiences, and responds to climate change as well as how to assess climate change risks in this sector. To this end, the Canadian mining sector's vulnerability to climate change has been extensively studied, as have the perceptions, attitudes, and adaptation and mitigation strategies of Canadian mining practitioners (Ford et al. 2010(Ford et al. , 2011;;Pearce et al. 2009Pearce et al. , 2011)). Similar research efforts regarding climate-change-related impacts, adaptation strategies, perceptions, and future expectations have been conducted in Australia (Loechel et al. 2013a, b;Loechel and Hodgkinson 2014;Sharma et al. 2013;Sharma and Franks 2013). Finally, recent scientific efforts have resulted in a probabilistic framework for the assessment of climate-change-related risks at a local (i.e., site) level (Mavrommatis et al. 2019).

The work reported in the present paper aimed to add to the abovementioned scientific literature by exploring the impacts of the changing climate on the Greek mining sector. More specifically, a survey based on a bottom-up approach was performed to explore the perceptions and attitudes of Greek mining practitioners about the present (perceived) and future (anticipated) impacts of climate change, as well as to examine adaptation and mitigation actions that have already been or are scheduled to be undertaken by mining companies to address this issue. The rest of the paper is structured as follows. The next section describes the methodology used in this research. The results of the survey are then presented. Finally, the main findings are discussed, and conclusions are drawn from the results of the survey.

div.head: Study area
div.p: According to Moustakas et al. (2016Moustakas et al. ( , 2018)), the Greek mining sector plays an important role in mineral production worldwide. Several hundred business entities across the country produce bauxite, nickel, caustic calcined magnesite, marble, perlite, bentonite, pumice, lignite, and mixed sulfide-oxide gold, silver, copper, lead, and zinc ores (Tzeferis 2015; Department for the Development and Policy Analysis of Minerals and Raw Materials 2018). Greece is the leading bentonite producer in Europe and the world's leading producer of unexpanded perlite. Although its importance to the national economy has decreased over the past three decades, mining still contributes 3.4% of the Greek gross domestic product (GDP), with a turnover of €6.2 billion (Moustakas et al. 2016). Mining is also an important source of direct investment and employment, as well as an economic pillar for local economies and regional development (Moustakas et al. 2016).

The present research focuses in particular on the Cyclades (an island group in the Aegean Sea), where numerous mining companies have been operating for decades. In terms of mineral products, the mines on the Cyclades generate impressive amounts of major mineral commodities such as perlite, bentonite, kaolin, pozzolan, silicate, and zeolite (extracted on the islands of Milos and Kimolos), marble (from Tinos, Naxos, and Paros), as well as shale slabs and aggregates. The most important deposits of bentonite and perlite in Greece are located on Milos, and almost 1.5 million tons of bentonite and perlite are exported annually from Milos by just one company (Mavrommatis and Menegaki 2017). In terms of size, the mining companies that operate in the Cyclades encompass micro-sized single-person limited liability companies and family-type businesses with low production levels and an annual turnover of a few thousand euros as well as large multinational corporations that are listed on international stock exchanges and employ hundreds of personnel, have annual production levels of millions of tons, and have turnovers of hundreds of millions of euros. Thus, focusing on mining companies in the Cyclades allowed us to draw conclusions about the effects of climate change on a wide variety of Greek mining companies.

div.head: Survey design
div.p: In order to collect the required information, a survey questionnaire that included both closed and open-ended questions was administered via face-to-face semi-structured interviews to selected key practitioners of all the companies located in the study area. A list of all the extractive enterprises operating in the Cyclades was provided by the South Aegean Prefecture. More specifically, at the end of 2012, eight, seven, five, and three mining companies were operating on the islands of Naxos, Milos, Tinos, and Paros, respectively. There were also two mining companies each on the islands of Kea and Sifnos and one on each of Kimolos, Kythnos, and Syros. Based on the European Union's (EU) definition of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) (European Commission 2015) and each company's headcount, 25 of those 30 companies were considered to be microsized, 4 were considered to be small sized, and one was considered to be a large enterprise. It should be noted that there are companies that operate on more than one island, as well as companies that also have mining activities outside the Cyclades. Finally, there are companies that have many mining activities on the same island-many active quarries, multiple operations, and different mineral commodities.

The survey questionnaire (which is available to view in the Electronic supplementary material, ESM) was divided into three distinct sections. The first section explored the current climate-change vulnerability of the company that the respondent was associated with. The scope was to investigate whether the sampled mining companies have been affected by previous climatic events and to collect useful data on the financial impact of climate change and potential climate adaptation measures. More specifically, question 1 investigated whether mining companies have been affected by climate-related events and to what extent. Participants were provided with a list of severe phenomena that affect Greece according to Giannakopoulos et al. (2009). Question 2 explored the vulnerability of mining activities to the indicated phenomena, and question 3 collected quantitative data on each of the indicated phenomena (e.g., frequency, cost of the impacts of the phenomenon, cost of adaptation measures deployed, etc.).

The second section of the questionnaire investigated the awareness, attitudes, perceptions, and beliefs of the respondents regarding changes in the local climate over the past 10-20 years and predicted changes over the next 20-30 years. In particular, question 4 examined the participants' knowledge of global climate change and its consequences. Question 5 explored awareness of previous climate change; it asked respondents to report the changes that they have observed in the local climate (if any) in terms of intensity, frequency, duration, etc. The climatic events considered were wind, droughts, rainfall, snowfall, and temperature. Questions 6 and 7 asked respondents to express their beliefs about the potential impact of future climate change on their activities. Questions 8, 8a, and 8b examined perceptions of adaptation, past or scheduled adaptation measures, adaptation strategies, and barriers to adaptation. Questions 9, 9a, and 9b probed attitudes to mitigation, past or scheduled mitigation measures, and drivers of mitigation. Questions 10-12 documented participants' attitudes and perceptions regarding the significance of climate change and the vulnerability of their operations and facilities to climate change using a series of closedended questions. Finally, the third section included a set of demographic questions.
Upon completion of the design of the questionnaire, pilot pretesting sessions took place with mining practitioners to assess the clarity and appropriateness of each question.

div.head: Survey administration and analysis
div.p: Data collection began in February 2014 and was completed in August 2014. As mentioned above, the surveyed population included 30 mining companies operating in the Cyclades. Each company was contacted by telephone and, after explaining the scope of the survey, an appointment was made with the selected practitioner(s). In total, 41 mining practitioners affiliated with 30 companies were interviewed. More specifically, for family-type businesses, only one person-the owner (who was also the decision maker)-was interviewed. For larger companies and those with operations on more than one island, more than one person in the company (e.g., production managers, financial managers, etc.) was interviewed. The interviews were conducted on the premises of each company. The average interview time was about 1 h.

The data collected were entered into a database and then transferred to statistical software for further analysis. Univariate and bivariate statistical analyses were conducted to provide a summary of the data collected from the survey and to determine the potential empirical relationships between critical variables. Given the relatively small sample size, Fisher's exact tests were performed instead of chi-squared tests to examine the significance of associations between variables of interest.

The most commonly used significance level, p = 0.05 (i.e., 5%), was adopted. A p value of less than 0.05 indicates strong evidence that the null hypothesis is incorrect (i.e., that there is no correlation between the two variables), as there is less than a 5% probability that the null hypothesis is correct. The smaller the p value, the stronger the evidence for rejecting the null hypothesis.

div.head: Sample characteristics
div.p: Table 1 summarizes the main characteristics of the surveyed practitioners. The average age of the respondents was about 49 years old, and respondent ages ranged from 30 up to 80 years old. More specifically, 36% of the respondents were under 40 years old, 47% were between 41 and 60, and 17% were more than 60 years old. The respondents had been working in the mining sector for an average of 25 years (16% had been working in the sector for up to 10 years, 16% for between 10 and 15 years, 40% for between 16 and 30 years, and 28% for more than 30 years), indicating that the practitioners who participated in the survey had considerable experience in the mining sector. Furthermore, the majority of the respondents were well educated-more than 60% had completed tertiary education, whereas 22% of the respondents had minimal primary education. More than half of the respondents (56%) were owners of the mining company, 29% were mine engineers who were responsible for the day-to-day operations of the mine, and the rest had executive roles (e.g., mine planning manager, processing manager, operation manager, etc.).

div.head: Exposure to climatic events
div.p: Mining companies in the Cyclades are vulnerable to climate-induced extreme events. Among the 41 survey respondents, 34 (83% of all respondents) replied that heavy rainfall and storms have negatively affected their business (Fig. 1). Moreover, 31 respondents (76%) said that they are affected by extreme, stormy winds, 21 (51%) by heat waves during the summer season, and 12 (29%) by cold spells during the winter season. It was found that mention of heat waves was positively correlated with respondent age (p = 0.033) and work experience (p = 0.028), and mention of cold spells was correlated with work experience (p = 0.011). There were no other significant associations with demographic characteristics such as role in the mining enterprise, educational

Table level, or location of the mining activity. This implies that weather-related experiences are mainly associated with time-related characteristics such as respondent age and work experience, in agreement with previous studies which found that the beliefs of mining practitioners are shaped mainly by their past experiences (e.g., Ford et al. 2011). Furthermore, provided that the study area (i.e., the region within the Cyclades) was relatively small, there was no association with the location of the mining activity, implying that all of the islands are affected by more or less the same weather conditions due to their proximity to each other. Seventy percent of the respondents said that the impacts of the phenomena they had experienced were moderately or strongly affecting their operations. On the contrary, 10% of the interviewees reported being unaffected. The severity of past impacts was found to be correlated with the size of the company (p = 0.006). The latter may indicate that the size of the company affects the degree of awareness of its personnel.

div.head: Frequency and cost of climate-induced events and company vulnerability and adaptation
div.p: Each practitioner was asked to estimate the frequency and cost of climate-induced events as well as the vulnerability of their company to such events. In terms of the frequency, the participants provided the number of days or number of incidents per year for the most frequently occurring events. For less frequent phenomena, the interviewees provided the corresponding estimates for the last ten years. This resulted in mean annual frequencies of less than 1 for some risks (e.g., wildfires) that are expressed in days or incidents (

Table 2). On average, respondents reported 11 days of intense rainfall and 31 days with extremely windy weather per year. Furthermore, the practitioners reported 9 days per year with extremely high temperatures and 6 days per year with extremely low temperatures. Some practitioners have stated that, for certain extremely intense events, these disruptions led to the total suspension of all operations for several days. These impacts imposed a significant financial burden on the surveyed mining companies. For example, based on the estimates provided by several participants, the average annual cost of the effects of intense rainfall ranged from €50,000 for small companies to €150,000 for large corporations with multiple mining sites and intensive mining activities, while the costs of windstorms ranged from €35,000 to €115,000 for small and large companies, respectively (Table 3).

The last part of question 3 investigated the adaptation actions that the participating mining professionals have implemented in their companies along with their estimates for the cost of each measure. The adaptation actions could be split into two broad categories: soft and hard adaptation measures. Some participants suggested, for example, that the increased risk to machinery and equipment from extreme rainfall and flooding events had been addressed through the movement of all assets to a safe shelter before the event. Others highlighted the importance of carefully designing haul road networks (i.e., of ensuring the proper inclination and drainage of such networks). Several respondents reported hard adaptation measures such as the construction of culverts, silos, and garages. The majority of the adaptation actions undertaken were intended to tackle problems caused by excessive rainfall and strong winds. Table 4 presents a selection of the most distinctive hard adaptation actions that mining companies on the Cyclades have undertaken, as well as their implementation costs.

Answers to questions on the scientific knowledge of the surveyed Greek practitioners regarding climate change revealed that 17 of the interviewees (42%) were able to state only one of the above five concepts, 10 respondents (24%) stated only two of the above concepts, and 34% of the respondents could identify three or more of the above concepts. Climate change knowledge was found to be associated with past events (p = 0.006) and education level (p = 0.019). Further, associations were found between scientific knowledge of climate change, the age (p = 0.009) and experience (p = 0.041) of the respondent, and the size of the company (p = 0.002).

Regarding respondents' observations of local changes in climate during the past 10-20 years, 45 distinct responses were stated by 23 practitioners. The most commonly reported climate-change event was an increase in temperature (18%), followed by changes in rainfall intensity and frequency (Table 5). Older respondents (p = 0.039) and those with more work experience (p = 0.009) recalled more climatechange events. In fact, 20 out of the 23 interviewees had worked for more than 16 years in the mining sector. There were no other significant relationships between perceived local climate change and other respondent characteristics.

The beliefs and expectations of the respondents regarding the impacts of future climate change were strongly polarized (Table 6). In particular, 39% of the respondents (16 out of 41 respondents) believe that they will be negatively affected, while the same proportion believe that they will not be affected at all. Interestingly, 9 respondents (about 22%) expect that climate change will be advantageous due to milder winters, which will allow extended operating times and reduce operating costs associated with the drying process. The main reason for the more pessimistic beliefs about future climate change was the practitioners' experiences of previous adverse climatic events. Those who have a neutral or optimistic stance believe that changes in the future climate will have an insignificant or no impact on their mining activities (11 respondents or 27%), and that the small size of their operations will prevent them from being negatively impacted (9 respondents or 22%). It is noteworthy that respondents from large operations believe that future climate change will affect them positively (p = 0.005). Only 5 out of 41 respondents (12%) said that they expected future climate-change impacts to be highly significant. Interestingly, 3 out of those

The majority of the respondents (i.e., 41%) expect moderately significant impacts of future climate change. Finally, 11 respondents (i.e., 27%) believe that the impacts will be of low significance, and the rest (8 respondents or 20%) expect the impacts to be insignificant. There were no significant associations between beliefs and expectations and respondent characteristics. For questions 10 and 11, the participants were shown a projected climate-change scenario and asked to (a) identify if the predicted changes would affect their operations and (b) indicate which aspects of their operations they believed would be most impacted. In order to assess the most harmful climate regime changes for the mining sector, the participants' responses were scored using a four-level scoring scale (a score of 4 corresponded to "very important" or "very vulnerable" and a score of 0 to "not at all important" or "not at all vulnerable"). As shown in Table 7, which presents the total score for each climate-induced risk, the most harmful risks relate to extreme rainfalls and extreme winds, followed by heatwaves. Further, the most susceptible aspects of mine operations are mine quarrying, operations management (scheduling), road networks, machinery and equipment operations, waste and rehabilitation management, and loading/unloading processes. We observed that the findings on susceptibility to projected changes were quite similar to those reported in the first section of the survey regarding past climate-induced events. This indicates that the beliefs of mining practitioners are shaped mainly-maybe even solely-by their past experiences, a finding common in other similar studies (Ford et al. 2011).

Almost all of the respondents would like to know more about how the predicted climate in the mid-twenty-first century will impact their companies, the available options for climate-change adaptation, and their associated costs. Those who were more interested in this information were more likely to be older (p = 0.036). More scientific research on the impacts of climate change on the mining sector was moderately and strongly desired by 34% and 46% of the respondents, respectively. The respondents who sought out more research had been more seriously impacted by adverse climatic events in the past (p = 0.013), and believed that future climate change would affect them negatively (p = 0.037).

div.head: Climate-change adaptation measures, strategies, and barriers
div.p: The surveyed mining practitioners were asked to state if they had already implemented or planned to implement adaptation measures, and their reasons for doing so. Only 10 participants (24%) stated that they had already implemented adaptation actions to adjust to the impacts of climate change. An absence of previous adverse climate-change impacts and ignorance of the phenomenon were the most common reasons for not considering adaptation measures.

Those who reported that their companies had taken measures to adapt to climate change were additionally asked to characterize the nature of the measures as well as to identify the most common barriers to adaptation. The most commonly mentioned adaptation measures were engineering measures (e.g., the construction of culverts, drainage systems, pumping stations, and antilightning systems, the construction of new storage facilities, structural strengthening of ship loading facilities, and haul road enhancements). Three respondents (Table 8) mentioned behavioral measures (e.g., cleaning forests and moving machinery and heavy equipment to safer areas before storm events). Finally, four respondents reported technological measures, such as planning a new method of drying minerals. The most commonly reported barrier to adaptation was the cost of adaptation (38%), followed by the financial uncertainty (25%), and the uncertainty regarding climate-change impacts (17%).
Respondents also reported that institutional uncertainty, a short mine lifespan, and technological limitations were minor reasons for constraining adaptation actions (Table 8).

div.head: Actions aimed at mitigating climate change and mitigation drivers
div.p: Almost half of the participants (49%) said that their companies are taking action to reduce GHGs, while almost the same proportion said the opposite, with ignorance playing the predominant role (89%) in this polarized response (Table 8). When asked their reasons for choosing to mitigate, the respondents indicated that they did so for primarily economic reasons (33%), followed by moral (24%) and "obligatory" ones (24%). Interestingly, the economic driver for mitigation actions is a common finding in relevant studies worldwide (Ford et al. 2010). Among the respondents whose companies make efforts to reduce climate GHGs, the most common strategy for mitigating climate change (cited by 15 out of 20 practitioners, representing 52% of all strategies) was energy efficiency improvements achieved by replacing old machinery with newer equipment or by introducing heat exchangers to reduce wasted energy from exhausts. Other strategies implemented include the use of renewables (28%), carbon capture technologies (17%), and outsourcing of activities that release substantial emissions. Mitigation actions were found to be correlated with the mineral commodity (p = 0.007), the size of the company (p < 0.001), the educational level of the respondent (p = 0.016), and their professional relationship with the company (p = 0.005).

div.head: Discussion and conclusions
div.p: Previous research efforts based on top-down estimates indicate that the Greek mining sector may be sensitive to climate change. This is an issue that deserves attention, since the extractive industry plays an important role

Analysis of the latest publicly available data (HNMS 2019) covering the period 1975-2004 for two islands in the Cyclades, namely Naxos and Milos, shows that (i) the average mean annual temperature is currently 18.14 °C for Naxos and 17.57 °C for Milos, and the maximum and minimum daily temperatures of these islands are trending upwards, (ii) the average total precipitation per year for Naxos and Milos, which is currently 551 mm and 601 mm, respectively, is increasing slightly, and (iii) the maximum wind speed is decreasing slightly (wind speeds currently average 13 knots). Further, over a 30-year period, there has been an increasing trend in extreme weather events (defined as events below the 5th and above the 95th percentiles of the time series of recorded climate parameters). The frequency of extremely hot days with maximum daily temperatures exceeding the 95th percentile has doubled and tripled for Naxos and Milos, respectively. A similar trend is observed for extreme rainfall events (events exceeding the 95th percentile of the precipitation time series), which agrees with the observations made by the participants in the present study (e.g., the damaging events of December 2002, February 2003, February 2011, December 2012, January and November 2014, September 2015, and January 2017). The degree of sensitivity to these events varies with the company and depends on factors such as company size, mineral product, and local characteristics (e.g., the scale of the mining activities).

The above findings are in accordance with relevant Canadian and Australian studies (Ford et al. 2010;Loechel et al. 2013a;Loechel and Hodgkinson 2014). Climate-induced phenomena represent an extra expense to mining companies during daily operations. For example, the delayed occurrence of the etesian winds-best known as the meltemi in the Aegean Sea during September to October (the prevailing winds in the Cyclades during the summer)-reduces the efficiency of the process of drying extracted industrial minerals in the sunshine. The estimated cost of drying the material by artificial means (i.e., the extra fuel costs) is €560,000 annually.

The survey also revealed that there is a deficit of scientific knowledge regarding climate change among mining practitioners. This is particularly apparent for the owners of small companies, despite their multifaceted and critical roles in the sustainability of their businesses. Moreover, many participants believe that future climate change will not affect them negatively. This is interesting considering that respondents from (mostly) small-sized companies stated that their operations were suspended for several days during adverse weather events. Increased demand for mining products will, inevitably, increase operating time, which, as stated by many interviewed practitioners, is negatively affected by climate-related events. This adverse possibility is not fully understood by small business' owners. It is also interesting that more than half of the respondents had already noticed and perceived local climate change. This makes us skeptical about the lack of association between experiences, perceptions, and expectations-an attitude similar to those of Australian mining companies, who may be inclined to "forget" their past experience and excessively discount the likely severity of future weather events (Loechel et al. 2013a).

Adaptation actions have mainly been implemented by companies that have already experienced some negative impacts of severe climate events. The respondents from these companies also believe that future climate change will affect them negatively. This finding coincides with those from relevant studies in Canada (Ford et al. 2010(Ford et al. , 2011)). Further, the survey showed that even when practitioners admitted that their companies had repeatedly been damaged by previous manifestations of climate change, they were reluctant to take any adaptation measures. This "adaptation deficit," as coined by Ford et al. (2010), is a common feature of the mining sector worldwide, and is the reason that the International Council on Mining & Metals (ICMM) is urging companies to carry out proactive rather than reactive adaptation (ICMM 2006(ICMM , 2013)). Nevertheless, some survey participants during the interviews provided specific examples of adaptive management that worked well for their companies, such as (i) carefully designing slopes to avoid damage from runoff when creating, for example, haul roads and flat areas, (ii) moving machinery and equipment to safe areas before predicted extreme weather events to protect them, (iii) cleaning surrounding forest areas before the summer period, and (iv) collecting, using, and reusing rainwater runoff. As also found in the present study, Ford et al. (2011) mention that many practitioners underreport adaptation actions; they probably consider these actions to be just another aspect of maintaining daily operations.

More than half of the respondents indicated that their companies are taking some mitigation actions, such as outsourcing electricity generation (which transfers the responsibility for emissions) and the widespread introduction of heat exchangers to harness wasted thermal energy from chimneys-an observation made in other studies too (Ford et al. 2010(Ford et al. , 2011)). This tendency for mitigation rather than adaptation can be easily explained by the fact that most mitigation measures involve efficiency enhancements, which have a positive outcome on the company's bottom line. Replacing old equipment with new, more efficient and more environmentally friendly equipment is a win-win adaptive management strategy that enhances the overall resilience of the business regardless of climate outcomes (Warren and Lemmen 2014).

It is worth noting that the timing of the survey coincided with an extremely politically and financially volatile period in Greece, so notions such as "climate-change adaptation" often sounded like a luxury to some struggling Greek mining practitioners. In any case, the present study revealed a number of knowledge gaps that present opportunities for future research initiatives. Therefore, the mining community would appreciate further scientific efforts to clarify how climate change could impact the sector at the mine site level. Furthermore, the mining industry wants scientists to focus their research on adaptation strategies based on robust economic and climatic data. If mining companies embraced these strategies as part of the daily operations, the sector could become more climate resilient in the future. The role of governments and institutional stakeholders in promoting the abovedescribed agenda should be emphasized, along with their responsibility to mainstream climate-change awareness and disseminate successful adaptation actions and methods to increase the future resilience of the mining sector.

Any conclusions drawn from the present study regarding the Greek mining sector in general should be approached with caution, given that the survey sample was limited to a specific region. Future research efforts that cover the entire Greek territory could include a more representative sample, with respondents including high-level employees as well as company owners and decision makers. Moreover, such research could be complemented by case studies focusing on economic data, which should lead to more robust conclusions regarding the impacts of climate change on and adaptation options of the national mining sector.
